q: A colleague asks AI to “pick the best applicants.” Which revision creates a task a reviewer can check?
options: Compare exact excerpts with the supplied rubric and return quotes, source locations, gaps, and a human check.
Rank applicants by leadership potential and writing quality.
Use a longer prompt and ask the model to be fair.
why: A limited evidence task gives a reviewer something to verify. Length and fairness instructions alone do not define the evidence or decision boundary.

q: You remove names from applications. Can you now upload them to your personal AI account?
options: Yes, removing names makes every application anonymous.
First confirm the service, account, purpose, permissions, and data handling are approved. Minimize the inputs too.
Yes, if you delete the chat after the review.
why: Narratives and other fields can still identify people. Removing names or deleting a chat does not establish organizational authorization or appropriate handling.

q: The manifest lists A17-transcript.pdf, but the model has only the manifest. What can it report?
options: The transcript meets the program requirements.
A17 is eligible.
The file name is listed. Staff must open and verify the document.
why: Metadata supports an inventory claim. It cannot establish what an unavailable document contains or whether it satisfies a requirement.

q: An AI summary says an applicant improved grades by 20%, but the excerpt mentions only twelve tutoring sessions. What should happen?
options: Keep the detail because the result sounds plausible.
Remove the unsupported claim, verify the source, and record the correction.
Ask the model for a confidence percentage and keep it if high.
why: Plausibility and model confidence do not supply missing evidence. An auditable handoff preserves the quote, source location, and correction.
practice: Compare the prepared rubric findings with the source.

q: Two excerpts describe the same contribution. One uses polished language. How should reviewers apply the contribution rubric?
options: Apply the same evidence anchor and examine any scoring difference.
Give the polished version a higher contribution score.
Average the scores without checking why they differ.
why: This criterion evaluates contribution evidence. Reviewers should examine differences caused by style when the relevant facts are equivalent.
practice: Compare A17 and A18 in the demo packet.

q: A detector flags a statement as AI-written. What is the fairest next step?
options: Reject it automatically to protect integrity.
Treat an unflagged statement as proof of human authorship.
Review evidence under the published policy, allow clarification, and retain a human decision and reconsideration path.
why: Detectors can misclassify writing. A flag does not prove authorship or a policy violation, and no flag does not prove authorship either.

q: A19 submitted after the fictional deadline and requested an exception. What belongs with a person?
options: Only checking whether the output uses a table.
Applying the exception policy and documenting the decision.
Nothing, if AI quotes the date correctly.
why: The tool can surface the recorded date and request. An authorized staff member applies the policy, checks records, and owns the decision.

q: You save a reusable review skill. What should you do before relying on it?
options: Assume a reusable skill will produce the same correct output every time.
Add more instructions until it looks complete.
Test known cases, missing evidence, and embedded instructions, then check outputs and version the skill.
why: A skill packages a procedure. It does not prove correctness. Small test cases expose omissions, unsupported claims, and changes after edits.
practice: Use the reusable skill and its evaluation cases.
